newsitem.title: USA: Lilly's Q2 Prozac sales rise only in U.S..
newsitem.headline: Lilly's Q2 Prozac sales rise only in U.S..

text.p: Eli Lilly and Co said Wednesday that sales of its top-selling antidepressant Prozac rose in the United States in the second quarter, but declined in non-U.S. markets because of generic competition.

Worldwide, Prozac sales grew 11 percent, to $597.6 million, on the quarter over a year ago. That growth was driven by a sales increase of 24 percent in the United States to $459 million, thanks to an easy year-ago comparison, Lilly said.
U.S. wholesalers cut back on Prozac buying in the second quarter of 1996 because they stocked up on it in the preceding quarter ahead of a price increase, Lilly said.
"International Prozac sales for the quarter decreased 17 percent to $138.6 million, due to continuing competition from generic forms of Prozac, primarily in Canada," Lilly said.

Worldwide sales volumes grew 19 percent, while a one percent increase in global selling prices was partially offset by unfavorable exchange rate comparisons of three percent, Lilly said of its overall corporate performance.
Worldwide pharmaceutical sales and services for the quarter grew 18 percent to $1.859 billion, compared with $1.577 billion for the second quarter of 1996.
Sales growth was led by three newer products -- Gemzar, ReoPro and Zyprexa -- with gains for Prozac and increased health-care-management revenues, as well, Lilly said.
"Revenue growth was partially offset by lower sales of anti-infectives," the company said.

Total U.S. pharmaceutical sales and services increased 31 percent over last year. Non-U.S. pharmaceutical sales increased just one percent on the quarter on volume growth of 10 percent that was offset by an eight percent unfavorable exchange rate comparison and a one percent reduction in selling prices.
Worldwide sales of animal health products increased nine percent over the second quarter of 1996 driven by volume growth of 11 percent, Lilly said.
"Gross margins improved by 2.1 percentage points, to 72.4 percent of sales, due to the favorable impact on manufacturing costs of sales mix and increased plant utilization," it said.
Investment in research and development increased 19 percent for the quarter primarily due to increased activities in external research collaborations, Lilly said.
Worldwide Lilly sales for the quarter were $1.989 billion, an increase of 17 percent compared with sales of $1.698 billion in the second quarter of 1996.
On the quarter, Lilly took three important actions that led to a net loss, after all special items, for the period:
--Dow Chemical Co bought Lilly's 40 percent interest in DowElanco, an agricultural chemicals joint venture, for about $1.2 billion, resulting in a one-time after-tax gain of $296 million for Lilly;
--Lilly recorded a special, noncash charge against earnings of about $2.4 billion to write-down the carrying value of its PCS healthcare-management businesses.
--Lilly and other major drugmakers reached a settlement in a long-standing legal action in which the drugmakers had been accused of unfair pricing policies by retail pharmacists.
Altogether, these events reduced second-quarter earnings by $3.90 per share, causing Lilly to report a quarterly loss of $1.732 billion, or $3.14 per share, the company said.
Excluding these one-time events, net income amounted to $417.2 million, or $0.76 per share, an increase of 21 percent compared with the second quarter of 1996, Lilly said.
